q1: Decision: start systemic therapy now rather than wait for the liquid biopsy (the family's request is reasonable given the growing residual on the 2026-12-12 MRI), and use single-agent oral temozolomide as the first choice - 150-200 mg/m2 on days 1-5 of a 28-day cycle (or continuous low-dose/metronomic 75-100 mg/m2/day if marrow reserve is a concern after 60 Gy) - with weekly CBC and a restaging MRI after about 4 cycles. Candidate chemotherapy options to weigh: (1) temozolomide - CNS-penetrant, convenient, modest toxicity, active across high-grade CNS neoplasms of several lineages, and the best risk-benefit bridge while the entity is unknown; this is what was started and it is being tolerated. (2) Lomustine (CCNU), alone or in a PCV-style combination - an alternative alkylator if temozolomide fails or MGMT promoter methylation is absent, but with heavier myelosuppression, hepatic and pulmonary toxicity after recent cranial radiotherapy. (3) Sarcoma-directed cytotoxic therapy - gemcitabine plus docetaxel, or an anthracycline-based regimen (doxorubicin +/- ifosfamide) - only if the pathology/behaviour proves to be that of a soft-tissue or meningeal sarcoma, since anthracyclines carry cardiac risk and no entity is established. (4) Bevacizumab, with or without an alkylator, as a non-conventional option for progressive enhancing/edematous disease and a phenotype that looks mesenchymal/angio-pericytic; it is anti-angiogenic rather than cytotoxic but fits the family's wish to look beyond conventional chemotherapy. (5) Trial enrollment at every step, and local salvage for the focal growing bed (re-resection or stereotactic re-irradiation) in parallel, because a systemic drug alone may not control a locally progressing residual. (6) Platinum/etoposide only if the phenotype shifts toward a carcinoma-like lineage, and intrathecal methotrexate only if CSF-confirmed leptomeningeal disease appears (currently none - the C6 pial nodule is stable). Key reasons for the ranking: the histologic entity and grade are still not established ('high-grade spindle cell/mesenchymal neoplasm, NOS', STAT6 negative, no NAB2-STAT6), so no entity-specific regimen can be claimed; therapy must be chosen by phenotype, patient factors (34 years, ECOG 1, marrow recently irradiated to 60 Gy/30 fx), and reversibility; and because molecular results are due within weeks, a tolerable, easily held regimen is preferred over committing to a prolonged toxic combination.
q2: Decision: no - do not add a second chemotherapy drug at this visit. Continue single-agent oral temozolomide at full dose, document tolerance and marrow counts, and reassess with the planned surveillance MRI (about 4 weeks, around the same time the ctDNA report returns) before changing anything. Reasons: (1) there is no evidence that adding a partner agent improves outcomes in an unclassified high-grade mesenchymal/spindle-cell neoplasm - the entity, grade, MGMT status and now the molecular profile are all unsettled, so combination therapy would be unprincipled guesswork; (2) temozolomide is being tolerated without significant toxicity and no radiographic progression on it has yet been shown, so the first task is to establish whether it is working, not to escalate; (3) the candidates for a second drug (lomustine, procarbazine, vincristine) are myelosuppressive, and adding them soon after 60 Gy to the resection bed risks cytopenias, infections and forced temozolomide dose reductions - a net loss; (4) the pending liquid biopsy may soon redirect therapy entirely, so an irreversible toxic combination started now could be wasted. Trigger and plan for escalation: if the on-treatment MRI shows progression, or if pathology/molecular results define a specific lineage, then at the tumour board choose - switch to or add lomustine (or PCV); dose-dense/metronomic temozolomide; bevacizumab +/- lomustine (particularly if the tumour looks solitary-fibrous-tumour/hemangiopericytoma-like or has prominent enhancement/edema); gemcitabine-docetaxel or doxorubicin-based therapy if a sarcoma phenotype is confirmed; or a clinical trial - alongside local options (second-look resection, stereotactic re-irradiation of the growing margin). If MGMT promoter methylation can be obtained on the archived block, use it to guide alkylator choice. Reserve earlier combination therapy for rapid clinical or radiographic deterioration on single-agent temozolomide.
q3: Decision: no - do not stop chemotherapy and do not switch to targeted therapy on this report alone. Continue temozolomide unchanged while the result is verified; take the report seriously and act on it only after confirmation. Reasons: (1) This is a single, unconfirmed peripheral-blood result. Plasma ctDNA from a CNS tumour sheds poorly across an intact blood-brain barrier, so a positive plasma call must be shown to derive from this tumour; blood-based variants can also reflect clonal haematopoiesis or a second clone. Sequence matched normal (buffy coat), repeat plasma, and test CSF tumour DNA (higher yield for CNS shed) before believing it is the tumour's genotype. (2) The pattern should raise the possibility of an extra-CNS primary rather than settle the CNS diagnosis: an FGFR2 fusion together with KRAS, STK11 and CTNNB1 is far more typical of certain peripheral carcinomas (for example FGFR2-rearranged cholangiocarcinoma, or KRAS/STK11 co-mutated lung adenocarcinoma) than of a CNS mesenchymal neoplasm. Restage with contrast CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (plus liver imaging/MRCP or PET as indicated), re-review the pathology with that in mind, and check the 2026-10-28 block. That work-up changes everything downstream and must come first. (3) The molecular finding alone does not establish the histologic entity - the diagnosis remains 'high-grade spindle cell/mesenchymal neoplasm, NOS'. None of FGFR2, KRAS, STK11 or CTNNB1 is defining for a WHO CNS mesenchymal tumour entity; the entity-defining test still outstanding is DNA methylation/epigenetic profiling on tissue, with RNA fusion testing and expanded immunohistochemistry. (4) There is no validated actionable indication here: FGFR inhibitors (pemigatinib, infigratinib, futibatinib and others) are approved for FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma and selected other tumours, not for unclassified CNS mesenchymal neoplasms; there is no tumour-agnostic approval covering these alterations, CNS penetration and efficacy of FGFR inhibitors in this setting are unproven, and KRAS/STK11 and CTNNB1 activation may mark resistant (mesenchymal/Wnt-driven, immunotherapy-poor) phenotypes rather than actionable dependencies. (5) The patient is doing well on temozolomide with no significant toxicity and has not been shown to progress on it; abandoning an effective, tolerated, CNS-penetrant drug on an unconfirmed blood result risks uncontrolled growth at the left frontal bed and further leptomeningeal/drop spread (a C6 pial nodule is already present). (6) Next steps: continue temozolomide; confirm each alteration in tumour tissue (macrodissected FFPE from the resection specimen - RNA fusion/FISH, IHC, targeted NGS); add CSF ctDNA and matched-normal sequencing; complete methylation profiling; restage systemically for a hidden primary; review at the molecular tumour board and look for a trial. Consider genotype-matched therapy only if an alteration is confirmed as tumour-derived AND a relevant trial or an approved agent with a defensible CNS strategy exists - ideally in a trial, with a pre-defined response-assessment plan and as a planned sequence with (not an abrupt replacement of) chemotherapy, while the histologic entity remains explicitly unestablished.
